note: Rabbi Yoḥanan met the young son of Reish Lakish and asked him what verse he had learned. The boy said: 'A tithe shall you tithe,' and asked what it meant. Rabbi Yoḥanan said: tithe so that you will become wealthy. Asked how he knew, he said: go and test it. The boy objected that one may not test God, and Rabbi Yoḥanan cited Rabbi Hoshaya: except here, as Malachi says, 'Bring the whole tithe... and test Me now by this.' The boy replied that had he reached that verse, he would not have needed Rabbi Yoḥanan or Hoshaya his teacher.
why: The Gemara has just quoted Rabbi Yoḥanan's reading of the verse: take a tithe so that you will become wealthy. This story shows a child challenging that very teaching; another story about the same boy follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Taught the boy that tithing brings wealth and defended it with a verse from Malachi.

people.name: the young son of Reish Lakish
people.about: A child who questioned Rabbi Yoḥanan sharply about the verse he had studied.

people.name: Rabbi Hoshaya
people.about: Quoted by Rabbi Yoḥanan; the boy calls him Rabbi Yoḥanan's teacher.

terms.meaning: A tenth of one's produce set aside as the Torah commands.
Demanding that God prove Himself; the Torah forbids it in Deuteronomy, 'You shall not test the Lord your God.'

note: Abba the Bloodletter received greetings from the heavenly academy every day, Abaye only every Friday, and Rava only on Yom Kippur eve. Abaye was upset and was told he could not do what Abba did: Abba treated men and women separately, gave women a slit garment so as not to see them exposed, and had a hidden box for fees so the poor were not shamed; he paid scholars instead of charging them. Abaye sent two Sages to test him. Abba hosted them; in the morning they took his rugs to the market. When asked to price them, he named what he had paid. He said he assumed they needed money to ransom captives, and that he had already given the rugs to charity. Rava, upset over Abaye, was told: your merit protects your whole city.
why: The Gemara has been telling of Sages who decreed fasts over plague. It now groups stories about the hidden merit of ordinary people; the story of the prison guard who saved women and warned the Sages follows.

people.name: Abba the Bloodletter
people.about: A bloodletter who received daily greetings from Heaven for his modesty, discretion and generosity.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage, greeted from Heaven each Shabbat eve, who sent two Sages to test Abba.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage greeted from Heaven only on Yom Kippur eve, and upset about Abaye's greater honor.

terms.meaning: The heavenly academy, imagined as a gathering of the Sages in Heaven.
An old medical treatment of drawing blood from a vein.
Paying to free captives, considered one of the most urgent forms of charity.

note: Rabbi Zerika told Rav Safra to see the difference between the powerful men of the Land of Israel and the pious men of Babylonia. When rain was needed, Rav Huna and Rav Ḥisda in Babylonia would say: let us gather and pray, perhaps God will send rain. But Rabbi Yona, father of Rabbi Mani, would tell his household he was going to buy grain, then go out, stand in a low, hidden place covered in sackcloth, and pray, and rain would come. When he came home and was asked for the grain, he said that now that rain had come, there would be relief in the world.
why: The Gemara is telling stories of righteous people whose prayers brought rain, such as Abba Ḥilkiyya and Ḥanan HaNeḥba, who also hid their greatness; stories about Rabbi Yona's son follow.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Draws the comparison between Sages of the Land of Israel and of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: With Rav Ḥisda, one of the pious men of Babylonia who prayed for rain in public.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: With Rav Huna, one of the pious men of Babylonia who prayed for rain in public.

people.name: Rabbi Yona
people.about: Father of Rabbi Mani; he prayed for rain in secret and hid it even from his family.

terms.meaning: Rough cloth worn as a sign of mourning or repentance.

note: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, a poor man, came to own goats, especially since the Sages forbid raising small animals in the Land of Israel. Rav Pineḥas explained: a man once left chickens at his door, and his wife found them. Rabbi Ḥanina told her not to eat their eggs. The chickens multiplied until they became a nuisance, so he sold them and bought goats. Later the owner passed by and told a companion he had left his chickens there. Rabbi Ḥanina asked for an identifying sign, the man gave it, and he took the goats. These were the goats that brought home bears on their horns.
why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's goats, accused of damaging fields, came home with bears on their horns; it now asks how he had goats at all.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa
people.about: A poor and righteous Sage who kept a stranger's lost chickens and returned their worth as goats.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's wife
people.about: Found the chickens left at their door.

people.name: Rav Pineḥas
people.about: Tells how Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa came to have goats.

terms.meaning: Sheep and goats, which the Sages barred from being raised in the Land of Israel because they graze in others' fields.
An identifying mark by which an owner proves that a lost item is his.

note: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decreed a fast for rain, and rain fell after sunrise. He thought to have the fast completed, but Rabbi Ami told him the rule is before noon or after noon. Shmuel HaKatan decreed a fast, and rain fell before sunrise; the people took it as praise of the community, but he said it was like a slave asking his master for a reward, and the master says: give it to him, so I do not have to hear his voice. Another time rain fell after sunset; again they took it as praise, and he said it was like a master who says: let him wait and suffer, then give it to him.
why: A baraita has just given three views on when rain that falls during a fast lets people stop fasting: sunrise, noon, or the ninth hour. Rabbi Ami rules by the noon view, and the Gemara then asks what Shmuel HaKatan would count as praise of the community.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: Decreed a fast for rain and thought to complete it after rain fell after sunrise.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Told Rabbi Yehuda Nesia that the cutoff is noon.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: Decreed fasts for rain and twice told the people the rain was no sign of their merit.

terms.meaning: Ordered a public fast day, here to pray for rain in a drought.
A short illustrative story comparing one situation to another.
